dmm-2011-power-01.title: Divisors of a prime
dmm-2011-power-01.body:
The only positive divisors of $p$ are $1$ and $p$, so $\gcd(p,q)\in\{1,p\}$. But $p\nmid q$: the only divisors of the prime $q$ are $1$ and $q\ne p$. Hence $\gcd(p,q)=1$.

**Answer: 1**

dmm-2011-power-02.title: Use $n\cdot1=n$
dmm-2011-power-02.body:
Since $f$ is not always zero, pick $n$ with $f(n)\ne0$. As $\gcd(n,1)=1$, multiplicativity gives $f(n)=f(n\cdot1)=f(n)f(1)$. Dividing by $f(n)\neq0$ gives $f(1)=1$.

**Answer: 1**

dmm-2011-power-03.title: Divisors of a product of coprime numbers
dmm-2011-power-03.body:
*Multiplicative.* Let $\gcd(m,n)=1$. Every divisor $d$ of $mn$ can be written uniquely as $d=d_1d_2$ with $d_1=\gcd(d,m)\mid m$ and $d_2=\gcd(d,n)\mid n$ (the primes of $d$ split according to whether they divide $m$ or $n$, since $m,n$ share no prime). Conversely any $d_1\mid m$, $d_2\mid n$ give the divisor $d_1d_2$ of $mn$, and different pairs give different products because the factors are coprime. So divisors of $mn$ correspond bijectively to pairs of divisors, and $t(mn)=t(m)t(n)$. Also $t(1)=1\neq0$, so $t$ is not identically zero.

*Not totally multiplicative.* $t(2\cdot2)=t(4)=3$ (divisors $1,2,4$), but $t(2)t(2)=2\cdot2=4$.

**Answer: multiplicative, but not totally multiplicative.**

dmm-2011-power-04.title: The value $L=1$ works
dmm-2011-power-04.body: Since $f$ is increasing and $n<n+p$, we have $f(n+p)\ge f(n)$ for every natural $n$, in particular for every $n$ relatively prime to $p$. So $L=1$ satisfies the defining condition, and $G(f,p)$, the *greatest* real number satisfying it, is at least $1$. (The defining condition is meaningful because $f(n)>0$ for all $n$: $f(1)=1$ and $f$ is increasing.) ∎

dmm-2011-power-05.title: Induction on $k$
dmm-2011-power-05.body:
Write $G=G(f,p)$. For $k=1$ this is the definition of $G$ (as $n$ is relatively prime to $p$). Suppose $f(n+kp)\ge G^kf(n)$. Since $\gcd(n+kp,p)=\gcd(n,p)=1$, the definition of $G$ applied to $n+kp$ gives $f(n+(k+1)p)\ge G\,f(n+kp)$. Both $G$ and $f(n)$ are positive, so
$$f(n+(k+1)p)\ge G\cdot G^kf(n)=G^{k+1}f(n).\ ∎$$

dmm-2011-power-06a.title: Compare $f(n+kp)$ with $f(2n)$
dmm-2011-power-06a.body:
Fix $k$ and write $G=G(f,p)$. Choose $n$ with $n\equiv1\pmod{2p}$ and $n>kp$ (for example $n=2p(k+1)+1$). Then $n$ is odd and relatively prime to $p$.

By the previous problem, $f(n+kp)\ge G^kf(n)$. On the other hand $n+kp<2n$ because $n>kp$, so, $f$ being increasing, $f(n+kp)\le f(2n)$. Since $n$ is odd, $\gcd(2,n)=1$, hence $f(2n)=f(2)f(n)$. Therefore
$$G^kf(n)\le f(n+kp)\le f(2)f(n),$$
and dividing by $f(n)>0$ gives $G^k\le f(2)$. ∎

dmm-2011-power-06b.title: Powers cannot stay bounded unless $G\le1$
dmm-2011-power-06b.body: If $G=G(f,p)>1$, then $G^k\to\infty$ as $k\to\infty$, so $G^k$ would eventually exceed the fixed number $f(2)$, contradicting $G^k\le f(2)$ for all $k$. Hence $G\le1$. Together with $G\ge1$ this gives $G(f,p)=1$. ∎

dmm-2011-power-07a.title: Rewrite products of coprime numbers
dmm-2011-power-07a.body:
*First inequality.* It is equivalent to $f(p^{k+1})f(n)\le f(p^k)f(np+1)$ (both $f$-values are positive). Since $\gcd(n,p)=1$, $f(p^{k+1})f(n)=f(np^{k+1})$. Since $\gcd(np+1,p)=1$, $f(p^k)f(np+1)=f(p^k(np+1))=f(np^{k+1}+p^k)$. As $np^{k+1}<np^{k+1}+p^k$ and $f$ is increasing, $f(np^{k+1})\le f(np^{k+1}+p^k)$.

*Second inequality.* It is equivalent to $f(np+1)\le f(p)f(n+p)$. Since $\gcd(n+p,p)=\gcd(n,p)=1$, $f(p)f(n+p)=f(p(n+p))=f(np+p^2)$, and $np+1\le np+p^2$, so $f(np+1)\le f(np+p^2)$. ∎

dmm-2011-power-07b.title: Same idea, now from below
dmm-2011-power-07b.body:
*First inequality.* We need $f(p)f(n-p)\le f(np-1)$. Since $n-p\ge1$ and $\gcd(n-p,p)=\gcd(n,p)=1$, $f(p)f(n-p)=f(p(n-p))=f(np-p^2)$, and $np-p^2\le np-1$, so $f(np-p^2)\le f(np-1)$.

*Second inequality.* We need $f(np-1)f(p^k)\le f(n)f(p^{k+1})$. Since $\gcd(np-1,p)=1$, $f(np-1)f(p^k)=f(p^k(np-1))=f(np^{k+1}-p^k)$, and since $\gcd(n,p)=1$, $f(n)f(p^{k+1})=f(np^{k+1})$. As $np^{k+1}-p^k<np^{k+1}$, $f$ increasing gives the inequality. ∎

dmm-2011-power-07c.title: Use that $G$ is the infimum of the ratios
dmm-2011-power-07c.body:
By definition $G$ is the largest $L$ with $f(n+p)/f(n)\ge L$ for all $n$ relatively prime to $p$, so $G$ is the infimum of these ratios. Hence for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a natural number $m$ relatively prime to $p$ with $f(m+p)/f(m)<G+\varepsilon$ (otherwise $G+\varepsilon$ would also be an admissible $L$).

*Upper bound.* Take $n=m$ in the first inequality: $\dfrac{f(p^{k+1})}{f(p^k)}\le f(p)\dfrac{f(m+p)}{f(m)}<f(p)(G+\varepsilon)$. Since $\varepsilon>0$ is arbitrary, $\dfrac{f(p^{k+1})}{f(p^k)}\le f(p)G$.

*Lower bound.* Take $n=m+p>p$ in the second inequality (it is relatively prime to $p$): $\dfrac{f(p^{k+1})}{f(p^k)}\ge f(p)\dfrac{f(m)}{f(m+p)}>\dfrac{f(p)}{G+\varepsilon}$. Letting $\varepsilon\to0$ gives $\dfrac{f(p^{k+1})}{f(p^k)}\ge\dfrac{f(p)}{G}$. ∎

dmm-2011-power-07d.title: Prime powers, then arbitrary products
dmm-2011-power-07d.body:
With $G=1$ we get $\dfrac{f(p^{k+1})}{f(p^k)}=f(p)$ for all $k\ge1$, so by induction $f(p^k)=f(p)^k$ for every prime $p$ and $k\ge1$.

Now let $m,n$ be any natural numbers. Write $m=\prod p^{a_p}$ and $n=\prod p^{b_p}$. Because $f$ is multiplicative and the prime powers are pairwise relatively prime,
$$f(mn)=\prod_pf\!\left(p^{a_p+b_p}\right)=\prod_pf(p)^{a_p+b_p}=\prod_pf(p)^{a_p}\prod_pf(p)^{b_p}=f(m)f(n).$$
So $f$ is totally multiplicative. ∎

dmm-2011-power-08.title: Suppose all values were integers
dmm-2011-power-08.body:
Suppose $f$ takes only natural-number values and $f(2)=3$. Then $f(2^j)=3^j$ and $f(3^m)=a^m$ where $a=f(3)$ is a natural number.

* $9>8$, so $f(9)\ge f(8)$: $a^2\ge27$, hence $a\ge6$.
* $27<32$, so $f(27)\le f(32)$: $a^3\le3^5=243$, hence $a\le6$ (since $7^3=343>243$).

So $a=6$, i.e. $f(3)=6$. Now $3^5=243<256=2^8$, so $f(243)\le f(256)$, i.e. $6^5\le3^8$. But $6^5=7776$ and $3^8=6561$, so $7776\le6561$, a contradiction.

Hence $f(n)$ cannot be a natural number for every $n$. ∎

dmm-2011-power-09a.title: Choose $B$ large
dmm-2011-power-09a.body: Choose a natural number $B>\dfrac1{1-\alpha}$, so that $(1-\alpha)B>1$, i.e. $\alpha B+1<B$. Let $A=\lfloor\alpha B\rfloor+1$. Then $A$ is a natural number, $A>\alpha B$ by the definition of the floor, and $A\le\alpha B+1<B$. So $\alpha B<A<B$. ∎

dmm-2011-power-09b.title: Squeeze between powers of 2
dmm-2011-power-09b.body:
Since $f(1)=1$ and $f$ is increasing, $f(2)\ge1$. Let $\alpha=\log_2f(2)\ge0$, so $f(2)=2^\alpha$ and $f(2^j)=f(2)^j=2^{\alpha j}$ (total multiplicativity).

Fix $n\ge2$ and a natural number $k$, and let $m=\lfloor k\log_2n\rfloor$, so $2^m\le n^k<2^{m+1}$. Because $f$ is increasing and totally multiplicative,
$$2^{\alpha m}=f(2^m)\le f(n^k)=f(n)^k\le f(2^{m+1})=2^{\alpha(m+1)}.$$
Taking $\log_2$ and dividing by $k$:
$$\alpha\frac mk\le\log_2f(n)\le\alpha\frac{m+1}k.$$
As $k\to\infty$, $\frac mk\to\log_2n$ and $\frac{m+1}k\to\log_2n$. Therefore $\log_2f(n)=\alpha\log_2n$, i.e. $f(n)=n^\alpha$. The case $n=1$ is trivial ($f(1)=1$). ∎

dmm-2011-power-10a.title: Two coprime large arguments
dmm-2011-power-10a.body: Suppose $f(n)<0$ for some $n$. Since $f$ is decreasing, $f(k)\le f(n)<0$ for every $k\ge n$. Take $a=n$ and $b=n+1$, which are relatively prime and both at least $n$. Then $f(a)<0$ and $f(b)<0$, so $f(a)f(b)>0$. But $ab\ge n$ gives $f(ab)<0$, contradicting $f(ab)=f(a)f(b)$. So $f(n)\ge0$ for all $n$. ∎

dmm-2011-power-10b.title: Split by whether $f$ ever vanishes
dmm-2011-power-10b.body:
Let $f$ be decreasing and multiplicative; $f(1)=1$, $f\ge0$, and $f(n)\le f(1)=1$.

**Case 1: $f(n)>0$ for all $n$.** Then $g=1/f$ is multiplicative (not always zero), and increasing because $f$ is decreasing and positive. So $g$ is an IMF and $g(n)=n^\alpha$ with $\alpha\ge0$. Hence $f(n)=n^{-\alpha}$. Conversely, every $n^{-\alpha}$, $\alpha\ge0$, is decreasing and (totally) multiplicative.

**Case 2: $f(N)=0$ for some $N$.** Take $N$ minimal; $N\ge2$ since $f(1)=1$. As $f$ is decreasing and nonnegative, $f(k)=0$ for all $k\ge N$, and $f(k)>0$ for $k<N$.

If $N\ge4$, then $N-1$ and $N-2$ are relatively prime, both $<N$ (so $f(N-1)f(N-2)>0$), and $(N-1)(N-2)\ge N$ (this holds for $N\ge4$), so $f((N-1)(N-2))=0\ne f(N-1)f(N-2)$, contradicting multiplicativity. So $N\in\{2,3\}$: $f(1)=1$, $f(k)=0$ for $k\ge3$, and $f(2)=c$ with $0\le c\le1$ ($c=0$ is $N=2$, $c>0$ is $N=3$).

Such $f$ is multiplicative: if $\gcd(a,b)=1$ and $ab\ge3$, then either $a$ or $b$ is at least $3$ (the only coprime pairs with both $\le2$ are $(1,1),(1,2),(2,1)$, which have product $\le2$), so both sides $f(ab)$ and $f(a)f(b)$ are $0$. If $ab\le2$ the identity holds since $f(1)=1$. It is decreasing since $1\ge c\ge0$.

**Answer:** exactly the functions $f(n)=n^{-\alpha}$ ($\alpha\ge0$), and the functions with $f(1)=1$, $f(2)=c\in[0,1]$, $f(n)=0$ for $n\ge3$. ∎
